name: 后记
highlights: 作者赵巍2008年赴美国爱荷华州立大学建筑系任讲师
陈志华为研究课题总策划，李秋香为项目负责人及测绘主持人
研究组于2007年9月和12月先后两次到方岩进行测绘和调研
参与测绘及调研的人有：李秋香、赵巍、毛葛、孙娜，及建筑学院五年级的林永明、陈华
书中手绘插图由赵巍绘制，照片均由赵巍拍摄（除注明外）
content_zh:
北京奥运会前的那个夏天，当作者正在清华东门外租的板楼里埋头写作的时候，收到了来自美国爱荷华州立大学（Iowa State University）建筑系的邀请信，聘请去做讲师。兴奋之余，不免有许多忧虑。由于美国大学开学早，况且还要顾及找房子、买家具等事宜，需要在七月底离开北京，这比原定完成书稿的计划至少早了两个月。作者向李秋香、陈志华老师解释了情况，并表明希望能在美国继续完成书稿的意愿，他们表示非常理解和支持。李老师依旧用她一向和善的口气说，要注意身体，工作也要抓紧。陈老师只是在电话里语重心长地嘱咐，想把工作完成是好，但是不要拖。就这样，在数以万计的各国运动员、记者以及游客纷纷降落在崭新的T3航站楼的那个星期，作者匆匆地离开了。

在美国教书的工作远远要比想象得辛苦，也极具挑战性。整个秋季学期，每天都如同打仗一般。晚上一到家，赖在沙发上就什么都不想做了。由于周末经常还要给十几个学生改论文，所以很少能拿出时间来继续在清华乡土组未完成的工作。惭愧地说，辜负了李老师和陈老师的嘱托，把这件事拖了下来。去年年底之前，李老师来了一封信，客气地问工作进展如何。作者无言以对，于是下定决心无论如何要把这件事尽快做完、做好，也好给无数信任的人一个交代。转眼间，春季学期几近尾声，虽然外面时常还会下雪，但是至少心中的这块石头逐渐落了下来，可以翘首企盼姗姗来迟的春天了。

回想在清华的那些日日夜夜，包括去方岩测绘调研、回来整理以及日后写作的整个过程，心中依旧会感慨万千。这其中得到了许许多多来自各个层面的帮助，而这项工作也只有在整个研究团队的共同努力和协作下，才能最终完成。

在方岩的日子里，当地村民对工作给予了极大的支持和关照，让人深刻感受到了人与人之间以心换心的历程。当那些朴实的村民看到不论刮风下雨、一趟一趟地从老街上走过，当一边专心聆听、一边认真记笔记，当一次又一次的登门拜访，当把冲洗好的照片送到他们手里的时候，他们对作者的信任也随之增加。于是他们会把压在箱子底的宝贝翻出来给看，他们会把刚刚出锅的、准备孝敬祖宗的金团拿给吃，他们会把自家院里结的橘子塞到包里，他们会讲更多的故事给听。

印度著名建筑师查尔斯·柯里亚（Charles Correa）曾经说，如果我们留意一下人道主义者和环境主义者当前所关心的主要问题，例如生态系统的平衡，垃圾的回收和再利用，公众的参与，适宜的生活模式，本土技术的应用等，我们发现亚洲人民已经开始这样做了。乡土建筑留给我们的不仅仅是悠久的历史和灿烂的文化，更应该超越雕梁画栋与户牖之美，乡土建筑中的许多原则和做法足以给二十一世纪的建筑师们解决环境、能源以及资金问题一些启示，甚至是设计的灵感。

陈志华老师曾经感慨：乡土文化是中华民族文化中还没有充分开发的宝藏，没有乡土文化的中国文化是残缺不全的，不研究乡土文化就不能真正了解我们这个民族。乡土建筑是乡土生活的舞台和物质环境，它是乡土文化最普遍存在的、信息含量最大的组成部分……乡土建筑研究是乡土文化系统研究的基础。没有乡土建筑的中国建筑史也是残缺不全的。

作者很庆幸，能有机会把自己融入乡土文化这莽莽苍苍的大地上；能连续一个星期工作在黄河岸边，感受它的伟大；能坐在有几百年历史的塘边屋前，听年过古稀的老人讲他小时候的故事；能爬进大屋顶，给近人高的斗拱掸掸灰，和它合个影；能怀揣手炉，喝着略带甜涩的井水沏的新茶，翻看着手抄的家谱……

方岩作者会再去。要在重阳初八夜那晚和成百上千的人一起上方岩祭拜胡公大帝；也要在正月十四那天和老街上的程氏后人一起迎龙灯；还要争取参与更多类似的研究工作，让更多的人、特别是年轻人重视和参与到乡土研究工作中来；更要把经历和研究成果写成英文，把中国的乡土建筑推向全世界！

感谢永康市博物馆陈景馆长给予的各方面支持与帮助；方岩镇政府提供的大力协助；永康市的胡春鸿与方岩镇的程伯敦两位学者，以及王岳阳摄影家提供的地方资料；广慈寺前任住持僧允明与现任住持释明修讲述的广慈寺重要历史。还要感谢那些住在老街上的程氏后人，程崇舜、程镇康、程茂发、程振锋、程高明、程明星、程圣言、程人龙、程水保、倒插门到程家的应业湘、嫁到老街上的白珑珑和骆巧燕，还有许许多多没来得及记下名字的热心人。

陈志华为岩下老街研究课题总策划，李秋香为项目负责人及测绘主持人，赵巍撰写文字，由陈志华、李秋香指导修改。方岩老街的研究是一项集体共同完成的研究项目，研究组于2007年9月和12月先后两次到方岩进行测绘和调研，参与测绘及调研的人有：李秋香、赵巍、毛葛、孙娜，及建筑学院五年级的林永明、陈华。测绘图主要由赵巍、孙娜、毛葛、林永明和陈华完成，陈金花参加了部分测绘图的绘制修改。随后赵巍又先后两次前往方岩老街，进行调研资料的核实及补充收集。书中手绘插图由赵巍绘制，没有另外注明拍摄者的照片均由赵巍拍摄。

赵巍
2009年4月
艾姆斯（Ames），爱荷华（Iowa）
美国
content_en:
In the summer before the Beijing Olympics, while埋头 writing in a rented apartment outside Tsinghua's east gate, the author received an invitation from the Department of Architecture at Iowa State University to serve as a lecturer. Excitement was mixed with anxiety: US universities start early, and with finding housing and buying furniture, departure by the end of July was necessary—at least two months earlier than the planned book completion date. The author explained the situation to Professors Li Qiuxiang and Chen Zhihua and expressed the wish to continue writing in the US; they were understanding and supportive. Professor Li said, as always kindly, Take care of your health, but keep up the work. Professor Chen said earnestly over the phone, It's good to want to finish, but don't delay. And so, in the week when tens of thousands of athletes, journalists, and tourists arrived at the brand-new Terminal 3, the author left in a hurry.

Teaching in the US was far harder and more challenging than expected. The entire fall semester felt like daily battle. Coming home at night, collapsing on the sofa, nothing else got done. Weekends were often spent grading papers for a dozen students, leaving little time for the unfinished Tsinghua vernacular architecture work. Ashamed to say, the author failed Professors Li and Chen and let the work drag on. Before the end of last year, Professor Li sent a letter politely asking about progress. With no answer to give, the author resolved to finish the work well, no matter what, to deliver on the trust of so many people. By the end of spring semester, though snow still fell outside, the weight in the heart gradually lifted, and one could look forward to a belated spring.

Looking back on the days and nights at Tsinghua—surveying at Fangyan, organizing materials afterward, and the writing process—the heart remains full of emotion. Help came from many quarters, and this work could only be completed through the collective effort of the entire research team.

During the days at Fangyan, local villagers gave tremendous support and care, deeply demonstrating the exchange of trust between people. When the plain villagers saw the team walking the old street rain or shine, listening attentively while taking notes, visiting door to door repeatedly, and delivering developed photographs, their trust grew. They brought out treasures stored at the bottom of trunks, shared freshly steamed jin tuan meant for ancestors, stuffed homegrown oranges into bags, and told more stories.

The renowned Indian architect Charles Correa once said: If we look at all the major concerns of humanists and environmentalists today—balanced eco-systems, recycling of products, people's participation, appropriate life-styles, indigenous technology, etc.—we find the people of Asia already have it all. Vernacular architecture leaves us not only long history and splendid culture, but beyond the beauty of carved beams and painted windows, many principles and practices in vernacular architecture can offer inspiration—even design inspiration—to 21st-century architects solving environmental, energy, and financial problems.

Professor Chen Zhihua once reflected: Vernacular culture is an insufficiently explored treasure of Chinese culture; Chinese culture without vernacular culture is incomplete; without studying vernacular culture, one cannot truly understand our nation. Vernacular architecture is the stage and material environment of vernacular life, the most ubiquitous and information-rich component of vernacular culture... research on vernacular architecture is the foundation of systematic research on vernacular culture. Chinese architectural history without vernacular architecture is also incomplete.

The author feels fortunate to have immersed in the vast land of vernacular culture; to work for a week straight by the Yellow River, feeling its greatness; to sit before a centuries-old house by a pond, listening to an elder in his seventies tell childhood stories; to climb into a great roof, dust off a nearly human-height dougong, and take a photo with it; to hold a hand warmer, sip slightly sweet-bitter well-brewed new tea, and leaf through hand-copied genealogy books...

The author will return to Fangyan. To climb the mountain on the eighth night of the ninth month with hundreds to worship Hu Gong Dadi; to welcome the dragon lantern on the 14th of the first month with the Cheng descendants of the old street; to participate in more such research, encouraging more people—especially young people—to value and join vernacular research; and to write experiences and research results in English, bringing Chinese vernacular architecture to the world!

Thanks to Curator Chen Jing of Yongkang Museum; the Fangyan Town Government; scholars Hu Chunhong of Yongkang and Cheng Bodun of Fangyan; photographer Wang Yueyang; former abbot Monk Yunming and current abbot Shi Mingxiu of Guangci Temple; and the Cheng descendants of the old street—Cheng Chongshun, Cheng Zhenkang, Cheng Maofa, Cheng Zhenfeng, Cheng Gaoming, Cheng Mingxing, Cheng Shengyan, Cheng Renlong, Cheng Shuibao, Ying Yexiang (who married into the Cheng family), Bai Longlong and Luo Qiaoyan (who married into the old street), and many more whose names were not recorded.

Chen Zhihua was the general planner of the Yanxia Old Street research project; Li Qiuxiang was the project leader and survey director; Zhao Wei wrote the text, with revision guidance from Chen Zhihua and Li Qiuxiang. The research team surveyed Fangyan in September and December 2007. Participants: Li Qiuxiang, Zhao Wei, Mao Ge, Sun Na, and fifth-year architecture students Lin Yongming and Chen Hua. Survey drawings mainly by Zhao Wei, Sun Na, Mao Ge, Lin Yongming, and Chen Hua; Chen Jinhua participated in revising some drawings. Zhao Wei subsequently made two more trips to verify and supplement research materials. Hand-drawn illustrations by Zhao Wei; all photographs by Zhao Wei unless otherwise credited.

Zhao Wei
April 2009
Ames, Iowa
USA
